title: Spatially Gated Diffusion for LocalizedCounterfactual Chest Radiograph Editing

paper.title: Spatially Gated Diffusion for Localized Counterfactual Chest Radiograph Editing
paper.abstract: Abstract Editing a chest radiograph requires completing the requested change while preserving unrelated content. We study a latent diffusion editor with an instruction-independent source trajectory and an instruction-conditioned editing trajectory. A learned gate mixes their post-sampler candidates at each executed step, and a separate image-space mask composites the decoded proposal with the source. On 2,400 MIMIC-derived requests, 2,244 outputs met the joint target, preservation, quality, and coverage rubric (93.5%), and target completion was 97.4%. Joint validity exceeded a matched composition-only control by 1.7 percentage points (paired patient-cluster 95% interval, 0.6–2.8). At a fixed learned mask, the learned-gate proposal improved joint validity by 1.6 points (0.8–2.4); at a fixed learned proposal, the learned mask improved it by 2.6 points (1.7–3.5). Across three training seeds, mean joint validity was 93.5% with a 0.3-point sample standard deviation. A blinded 240-request assessment yielded adjudicated joint validity of 93.3% for the full editor and 91.7% for composition only. Protected-region mean absolute error decreased from 0.0190 in the raw proposal to 0.0075 after composition. These findings distinguish recurrent-gating effects on the proposal from preservation through final composition in the assessed cohort.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Counterfactual image editing asks how an existing image would appear under a specified change. For chest radiographs, the request may be to insert or remove a finding while retaining unrelated structures. Target completion alone is insufficient: an image can satisfy the instruction while modifying another finding or moving a support device. Conversely, copying the source can yield excellent preservation without carrying out the edit. A useful editor must balance these requirements within the same request. Diffusion models provide expressive image priors [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , and recent medical editors introduce spatial constraints and language conditioning [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Spatial maps can play different roles in these systems. A map may summarize attention after generation, restrict the denoising computation, or specify how a generated image is blended with its source. These roles have different implications for interpretation and evaluation. A visually plausible map alone does not demonstrate that its location controls the generated proposal. We couple a factual source trajectory with an instruction-conditioned editing trajectory. At each step, a learned gate mixes the two candidate next-state latents. The factual trajectory is independent of the requested edit, while the editing trajectory proposes the change. The decoder produces a raw proposal y y . A separate applied mask A A then combines y y with the original image x x to form x cf x_{\mathrm{cf}} . This design exposes two computational routes for spatial control: recurrent latent mixing and final pixel composition. The distinction motivates a factorial intervention. We cross proposals generated under the learned or replacement gate with applied masks constructed from either gate. Holding the applied mask fixed tests the proposal route; holding the proposal fixed tests composition. This avoids attributing an improvement caused by copying source pixels entirely to the learned latent computation. Our contributions are a source- and timestep-dependent gate for post-sampler mixing, an explicit separation of recurrent gating from image-space composition, and a paired intervention analysis of these two routes. Evaluation includes a matched composition-only control, patient-cluster uncertainty, multiple training seeds, and blinded image-level assessment. We use “counterfactual” to denote conditional visual editing; we do not infer a patient’s physiological response to an intervention.

sections.heading: 2.1 Spatial Control in Diffusion Editing
sections.text: Blended Latent Diffusion combines masked latent editing with preservation of source content [ 7 ] . DiffEdit derives editing masks from differences between conditional diffusion predictions [ 8 ] , and RePaint constrains generation using the known region of an image [ 9 ] . InstructPix2Pix learns instruction-conditioned transformations [ 10 ] . Thus, neither spatial masking nor source preservation alone constitutes the novelty of our method. The specific mechanism studied here is recurrent mixing of two candidate next states using a learned source-dependent gate, together with an intervention design that separates this computation from final composition.

sections.heading: 2.2 Medical Counterfactual Generation
sections.text: RadEdit uses edit and preservation constraints to generate controlled shifts for evaluating biomedical vision models [ 4 ] . InstructX2X combines region-specific editing with guidance maps and introduces the MIMIC-EDIT-INSTRUCTION benchmark [ 5 ] . Its spatial restriction is particularly relevant to our comparison: our learned gate must be evaluated against a matched composition-only control rather than justified solely by the presence of a localization map. PRISM studies high-resolution language-guided editing of disease and device features [ 6 ] . BiomedJourney uses longitudinal patient information for instruction learning [ 11 ] , illustrating the relevance of paired temporal data while leaving the distinction between observational changes and causal interventions intact. More recent approaches broaden the available control mechanisms. MedXEdit-GRPO applies reward-guided online optimization to medical editing [ 12 ] . Mask-guided attention regulation modifies anatomical and pathology-related attention during inference [ 13 ] . RadCF adapts foundation image models using a causal specialization framework and latent flow matching [ 14 ] . Causal-Adapter conditions a diffusion backbone on a structural causal model and intervened attributes [ 15 ] . Its causal formulation differs from our finding-conditioned visual editing: longitudinal image pairs do not identify patient-specific causal outcomes. These approaches broaden the relevant design space. Our measured mechanism comparison uses the composition-only control and the stated local reruns of RadEdit, InstructX2X, and PRISM.

sections.heading: 2.3 Interpretation and Evaluation
sections.text: DAAM associates generated regions with words through aggregated cross-attention [ 16 ] . Attention-based association does not automatically establish a faithful explanation [ 17 ] . Here the gate is intrinsic only in the computational sense that it enters the state update. A gate intervention measures functional sensitivity, whereas spatial overlap with an independent annotation measures agreement with a reference. Neither alone proves clinical correctness. MedEBench separates editing accuracy, context preservation, and visual quality [ 18 ] ; this supports evaluating multiple outcomes jointly. We also follow the distinction between task-specific measurement and broad validity claims emphasized by Metrics Reloaded [ 19 ] . Physiological counterfactual inference requires causal assumptions beyond an image-editing model [ 20 ] .

sections.heading: 3.6 Implementation
sections.text: The backbone is adapted from SDXL base 1.0 [ 21 ] ; attention layers use LoRA [ 22 ] . Table 2 specifies the configuration. In particular, the eight-channel concatenation is an adaptation of the pretrained source interface, not the native SDXL four-channel input. The factual and conditional paths share parameters, but maintain separate latents and conditioning. During the four-cell intervention, the source image, edit instruction, initialization noise, shared weights, DDIM grid, classifier-free guidance, and mask-construction policy are held fixed. The two trajectories are evaluated under identical requests and the same 100,000-step EMA checkpoint. The composition-only control is trained separately with the same backbone, data, optimization budget, and test requests; the three paired runs use seeds 17, 23, and 41. sections.heading: 4.1 Data Sources and Eligibility
sections.text: MIMIC-CXR-JPG v2.1.0 supplies the radiographs and structured labels [ 23 , 24 ] . MS-CXR v1.1.0 provides 1,162 image–sentence annotation pairs with phrase-linked bounding boxes on a subset of MIMIC-CXR [ 25 , 26 ] . The resources share patient ancestry; MS-CXR is neither an independent site nor a dense lesion-mask dataset. Our patient split is 80/10/10 for training, validation, and testing, with training-side MS-CXR supervision restricted to the corresponding training patients. The evaluation contains 2,400 requests from 1,200 patients across pleural effusion, cardiomegaly, edema, consolidation, atelectasis, and pneumothorax. Requests cover insertion and removal. The source-state eligibility rule excludes uncertainty and requires the requested operation to be compatible with the source. Label uncertainty must remain distinct from an explicit negative, as highlighted by CheXpert [ 27 ] . Patients may contribute multiple requests. We split patients before forming pairs and requests, retaining all images of a patient in one partition, including the MS-CXR subset. Test requests are balanced overall between insertion and removal.

sections.heading: 4.2 Evaluation Reliability
sections.text: We assessed image-level editing reliability on a common subset of 240 held-out requests spanning the six findings and both operation directions. Two readers blinded to method identity reviewed the outputs of each method under the same requests for target completion, unintended non-target change, structural and artifact quality, and joint validity. Disagreements were adjudicated, and we report pre-adjudication Cohen’s κ \kappa for the binary joint-validity decision. This assessment tests task compliance and visual plausibility rather than a patient’s physiological response.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: The mechanism and intervention results support a specific conclusion: learned spatial mixing influences the proposal produced during denoising, and final composition contributes an additional preservation route. Exact copying where A = 0 A=0 is useful but is an algebraic property of composition rather than evidence that the mask identifies the correct lesion. A method can also satisfy a frozen evaluator without producing a medically appropriate change, so outcome definitions and evaluator independence remain essential to interpreting the results. The local comparison does not establish universal superiority over the cited methods. Their published objectives, tasks, and metrics differ, and newer approaches such as RadCF, MedXEdit-GRPO, and attention regulation are discussed as related work rather than presented as measured local baselines. The closest methodological claim is the combination of learned recurrent mixing and a test that holds the final mask fixed. Spatial gating by itself has substantial prior art. The present analysis has several limitations. The main cohort and factorial results depend on the study rubric and its evaluators. Agreement with that rubric alone does not establish independent clinical validity. The grouped ablation controls do not separate their constituent perturbations, and the three training runs provide only a limited estimate of optimization variability. All requests derive from MIMIC, and MS-CXR is its subset, so the evaluation does not measure transfer to an independent institution. Longitudinal observational pairs can differ in acquisition, positioning, inspiration, treatment, and unrecorded findings. The reader study evaluates image-level task compliance rather than patient-specific causal validity; its 240 requests do not replace external-site validation. Copying source pixels outside the applied mask follows from the composition equation, whereas correct lesion localization and clinically plausible disease change remain empirical questions. Generated images are research artifacts, not patient-specific treatment outcomes.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied recurrent mixing of source and instruction-conditioned diffusion trajectories followed by image-space composition. On 2,400 requests, the full editor achieved 93.5% joint validity, exceeding composition only by 1.7 percentage points (paired patient-cluster 95% interval, 0.6–2.8). Fixed-mask and fixed-proposal interventions distinguished the contribution of each route. The reader assessment and three-seed evaluation complement these findings, but the evidence remains confined to the assessed MIMIC-derived cohort. External-site and clinical validation are required for broader use.

sections.text: The study uses de-identified, access-controlled radiographs under the applicable PhysioNet data-use agreement. Generated images do not depict observed future patient states and should not be presented as authentic clinical records or used to support patient care. Any release of derived images or checkpoints requires assessment of memorization, re-identification, and redistribution constraints. We study a latent diffusion editor with an instruction-independent source trajectory and an instruction-conditioned editing trajectory. A learned gate mixes their post-sampler candidates at each executed step, and a separate image-space mask composites the decoded proposal with the source. On 2,400 MIMIC-derived requests, 2,244 outputs met the joint target, preservation, quality, and coverage rubric (93.5%), and target completion was 97.4%. Joint validity exceeded a matched composition-only control by 1.7 percentage points (paired patient-cluster 95% interval, 0.6–2.8). At a fixed learned mask, the learned-gate proposal improved joint validity by 1.6 points (0.8–2.4); at a fixed learned proposal, the learned mask improved it by 2.6 points (1.7–3.5). Across three training seeds, mean joint validity was 93.5% with a 0.3-point sample standard deviation. A blinded 240-request assessment yielded adjudicated joint validity of 93.3% for the full editor and 91.7% for composition only. Protected-region mean absolute error decreased from 0.0190 in the raw proposal to 0.0075 after composition. These findings distinguish recurrent-gating effects on the proposal from preservation through final composition in the assessed cohort. Keywords: Chest radiography; counterfactual image editing; latent diffusion; spatial gating; image preservation; model interpretation. 1 Introduction Counterfactual image editing asks how an existing image would appear under a specified change. For chest radiographs, the request may be to insert or remove a finding while retaining unrelated structures. Target completion alone is insufficient: an image can satisfy the instruction while modifying another finding or moving a support device. Conversely, copying the source can yield excellent preservation without carrying out the edit. A useful editor must balance these requirements within the same request. Diffusion models provide expressive image priors [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , and recent medical editors introduce spatial constraints and language conditioning [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Spatial maps can play different roles in these systems. A map may summarize attention after generation, restrict the denoising computation, or specify how a generated image is blended with its source. These roles have different implications for interpretation and evaluation. A visually plausible map alone does not demonstrate that its location controls the generated proposal. We couple a factual source trajectory with an instruction-conditioned editing trajectory. At each step, a learned gate mixes the two candidate next-state latents. The factual trajectory is independent of the requested edit, while the editing trajectory proposes the change. The decoder produces a raw proposal y y . A separate applied mask A A then combines y y with the original image x x to form x cf x_{\mathrm{cf}} . This design exposes two computational routes for spatial control: recurrent latent mixing and final pixel composition. The distinction motivates a factorial intervention. We cross proposals generated under the learned or replacement gate with applied masks constructed from either gate. Holding the applied mask fixed tests the proposal route; holding the proposal fixed tests composition. This avoids attributing an improvement caused by copying source pixels entirely to the learned latent computation. Our contributions are a source- and timestep-dependent gate for post-sampler mixing, an explicit separation of recurrent gating from image-space composition, and a paired intervention analysis of these two routes. Evaluation includes a matched composition-only control, patient-cluster uncertainty, multiple training seeds, and blinded image-level assessment. We use “counterfactual” to denote conditional visual editing; we do not infer a patient’s physiological response to an intervention. 2 Related Work 2.1 Spatial Control in Diffusion Editing Blended Latent Diffusion combines masked latent editing with preservation of source content [ 7 ] . DiffEdit derives editing masks from differences between conditional diffusion predictions [ 8 ] , and RePaint constrains generation using the known region of an image [ 9 ] . InstructPix2Pix learns instruction-conditioned transformations [ 10 ] . Thus, neither spatial masking nor source preservation alone constitutes the novelty of our method. The specific mechanism studied here is recurrent mixing of two candidate next states using a learned source-dependent gate, together with an intervention design that separates this computation from final composition. 2.2 Medical Counterfactual Generation RadEdit uses edit and preservation constraints to generate controlled shifts for evaluating biomedical vision models [ 4 ] . InstructX2X combines region-specific editing with guidance maps and introduces the MIMIC-EDIT-INSTRUCTION benchmark [ 5 ] . Its spatial restriction is particularly relevant to our comparison: our learned gate must be evaluated against a matched composition-only control rather than justified solely by the presence of a localization map. PRISM studies high-resolution language-guided editing of disease and device features [ 6 ] . BiomedJourney uses longitudinal patient information for instruction learning [ 11 ] , illustrating the relevance of paired temporal data while leaving the distinction between observational changes and causal interventions intact. More recent approaches broaden the available control mechanisms. MedXEdit-GRPO applies reward-guided online optimization to medical editing [ 12 ] . Mask-guided attention regulation modifies anatomical and pathology-related attention during inference [ 13 ] . RadCF adapts foundation image models using a causal specialization framework and latent flow matching [ 14 ] . Causal-Adapter conditions a diffusion backbone on a structural causal model and intervened attributes [ 15 ] . Its causal formulation differs from our finding-conditioned visual editing: longitudinal image pairs do not identify patient-specific causal outcomes. These approaches broaden the relevant design space. Our measured mechanism comparison uses the composition-only control and the stated local reruns of RadEdit, InstructX2X, and PRISM. 2.3 Interpretation and Evaluation DAAM associates generated regions with words through aggregated cross-attention [ 16 ] . Attention-based association does not automatically establish a faithful explanation [ 17 ] . Here the gate is intrinsic only in the computational sense that it enters the state update. A gate intervention measures functional sensitivity, whereas spatial overlap with an independent annotation measures agreement with a reference. Neither alone proves clinical correctness. MedEBench separates editing accuracy, context preservation, and visual quality [ 18 ] ; this supports evaluating multiple outcomes jointly. We also follow the distinction between task-specific measurement and broad validity claims emphasized by Metrics Reloaded [ 19 ] . Physiological counterfactual inference requires causal assumptions beyond an image-editing model [ 20 ] . 3 Spatially Gated Editor 3.1 Task and Notation Let x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] H × W x\in[0,1]^{H	imes W} be a frontal radiograph. MS-CXR v1.1.0 provides 1,162 image–sentence annotation pairs with phrase-linked bounding boxes on a subset of MIMIC-CXR [ 25 , 26 ] .
